papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Relapse occurs in 10%–20% of children with hepatoblastoma and is associated with inferior outcomes, yet standardized management remains limited. Defining risk factors and relapse patterns, as well as the role of surgery, particularly transplantation, is critical to optimizing survival. A retrospective review was performed of patients aged 0–18 years diagnosed with hepatoblastoma from 2007 to 2024. Demographics, tumor characteristics, treatment course, relapse patterns, and outcomes were collected. Analyses included univariable and multivariable logistic regression, Kaplan–Meier survival estimation, and log‐rank testing. Among 135 patients, 98 (72.6%) achieved remission without relapse, 32 (23.7%) relapsed, and 5 (3.7%) experienced primary progression without remission. Older age, PRETEXT (pretreatment extent of disease) IV, metastatic disease at diagnosis, and macrovascular invasion were associated with relapse on univariable analysis, but only older age remained independently associated with relapse (adjusted odds ratio 1.27 per year, 95% confidence interval 1.05–1.53); PRETEXT IV and metastatic disease were not significantly associated with overall survival. Lung‐only relapse demonstrated favorable survival (100% alive), whereas combined liver and lung or extrahepatic relapse had poorer outcomes (40%–44% alive), although survival did not differ significantly across relapse sites ( p = 0.15). Of 54 liver transplant recipients, 44 underwent upfront transplantation, and 10 underwent salvage transplantation, with no significant difference in overall survival ( p = 0.90), although the salvage group was small. Relapse or progression after upfront transplantation occurred in 27% of recipients; lung‐only relapse again conferred favorable survival. Long‐term survival is achievable in relapsed hepatoblastoma, particularly for isolated pulmonary relapse. Older age, likely a surrogate for adverse tumor biology, was associated with relapse but did not preclude survival when aggressive multimodal therapy was used. Salvage transplantation achieved durable survival in selected patients and should be considered for unresectable intrahepatic relapse when extrahepatic disease is absent or controlled.

papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Introduction Phosphatidylinositol 3‐kinase catalytic subunit type 3 (PIK3C3) is central to autophagy, which supports cancer adaptation to environmental stresses and may contribute to drug resistance. KRAS ‐mutant cancers have been reported to require autophagy for survival. We investigated the influence of KRAS mutation status on the roles of PIK3C3 in colorectal cancer (CRC) cell viability and chemosensitivity in vitro, as well as its association with patient prognosis. Methods The clinical significance of PIK3C3 expression in relation to KRAS mutation status was evaluated by immunohistochemistry in patients with advanced CRC. Cell viability, colony formation, and spheroid formation assays were performed using CRC cell lines. Results In KRAS ‐wild‐type ( KRAS ‐WT) Caco‐2 and Colo320 cells, PIK3C3 and the KRAS/ERK pathway appeared to positively regulate each other. In contrast, PIK3C3 inhibition did not reduce p‐ERK levels or induce significant p62 accumulation in KRAS ‐mutant SW480 and HCT116 cells. PIK3C3 knockdown reduced cell viability but increased resistance to 5‐fluorouracil (5‐FU) in Caco‐2 and Colo320 cells, whereas the opposite effect was observed in SW480 and HCT116 cells. Transfection with a KRAS ‐mutant plasmid sensitized Caco‐2 cells to 5‐FU accompanied by reduced thymidylate synthase (TS) and β‐catenin levels following PIK3C3 inhibition. Clinically, high PIK3C3 expression was associated with KRAS mutation and poorer survival in patients with advanced CRC. Its adverse short‐term prognostic association was more pronounced in KRAS ‐mutant CRC than in KRAS ‐WT CRC. Conclusion Based on preclinical in vitro findings, PIK3C3 appears to support KRAS ‐WT and KRAS ‐mutant CRCs in different ways. Notably, PIK3C3 inhibition enhances 5‐FU sensitivity in KRAS ‐mutant CRC cells, potentially through TS regulation, and warrants further investigation as a therapeutic strategy.

papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Background Cancer incidence in Africa is projected to reach 2.1 million new cases annually by 2040. Current treatment guidelines remain largely based on pharmacogenomic data predominantly from European and Asian genetic profiles, potentially compromising safety and efficacy in African patients. However, limited clinical validation data, extreme intra‐population genetic diversity, and significant healthcare infrastructure barriers constrain the translational application of pharmacogenomics in Africa. Objective This review critically examines pharmacogenomic variants with established clinical actionability in cancer treatment, focusing on those with differential frequencies or African‐specific alleles, and evaluates the evidence base for their implementation in African healthcare settings. Methods We searched PubMed/MEDLINE, PharmGKB, dbSNP, and Google Scholar for peer‐reviewed studies reporting pharmacogenomic variants in African or African‐ancestry populations relevant to cancer therapeutics. We synthesised evidence from recent African and global studies on pharmacogenomic variants affecting commonly used chemotherapy agents. Results Several variants show marked frequency differences between African‐ancestry reference populations and European populations, including DPYD rs115232898 (2.06% vs. 0.00%), CYP2D6 * 17 ( 18.76% vs. 0% ), and CYP3A5 *6 (12.82% vs. 0%). However, many of these estimates derive primarily from African‐American datasets and should not be interpreted as representative of continental African populations. African‐specific variants such as CYP2D6 * 17 and DPYD rs115232898 are underrepresented in guideline development datasets. Intra‐African genetic diversity is the highest globally, with Khoi‐San populations harbouring extensive private variation, suggesting that no single pharmacogenomic panel will be universally applicable across the continent. Conclusion While pharmacogenomics holds substantial promise for personalising cancer treatment in Africa, its current translational readiness is limited by a critical lack of African‐specific clinical validation data. Priorities include multi‐site validation studies, development of African‐enriched genotyping panels, and integration of pharmacogenomic education into oncology practice. Implementation must be accompanied by ethical frameworks ensuring data sovereignty and equitable benefit‐sharing.

papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Background Polygenic risk scores (PRS) and lifestyle factors are associated with colorectal cancer (CRC), but whether their associations and joint effects vary according to age at CRC onset remains unclear. We evaluated age‐related heterogeneity in the associations of genetic risk and lifestyle with CRC and examined their additive interaction in early‐ and late‐onset CRC. Methods We analyzed data from 405,453 cancer‐free participants aged 38–73 years at baseline in the UK Biobank. PRS and a healthy lifestyle score (based on eight modifiable factors) were assessed. Age‐scale Cox proportional hazards models estimated hazard ratios (HRs) for CRC risk by age at onset. Heterogeneity across age intervals was assessed using likelihood ratio tests. Additive interaction was assessed using the relative excess risk due to interaction (RERI), and differences in standardized incidence rates were evaluated. Results During a median follow‐up of 13.65 years, 6620 CRC cases were identified. Compared with low genetic risk, high genetic risk was associated with HRs of 3.72, 3.32, 2.80, and 2.01 for CRC occurring at ages < 55, 55–64, 65–74, and ≥ 75 years, respectively, with significant heterogeneity across age intervals ( p for heterogeneity < 0.001). Compared with a favorable lifestyle, the corresponding HRs for an unfavorable lifestyle were 1.10, 1.50, 1.58, and 1.28, respectively, with evidence of overall heterogeneity ( p for heterogeneity = 0.015). For late‐onset CRC, positive additive interactions were observed for an unfavorable lifestyle combined with intermediate or high genetic risk, whereas no such interaction was detected for early‐onset CRC. Conclusions The associations of genetic susceptibility and baseline lifestyle with CRC varied according to age at onset. Positive additive interaction between genetic risk and an unfavorable lifestyle was observed for late‐onset but not early‐onset CRC. These findings provide further evidence that the relative and joint associations of genetic and lifestyle factors with CRC vary across the life course.

papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Background The Observational Medical Outcomes Partnership Common Data Model (OMOP CDM) is a data standard that enables multicenter research. Primary objective was to describe the magnitude of healthcare utilization in pediatric cancer versus non‐cancer patients. Secondary objective was to compare 6‐month clinical outcomes related to abnormal lab tests and mortality. Methods In this multicenter retrospective study, we included pediatric patients 0–18 years at first medication administration. Cancer patients had a malignant neoplastic disease diagnosis and received chemotherapy. Index date was the first chemotherapy date. Non‐cancer patients were assigned analogous index dates based on randomly sampled first medication to chemotherapy intervals. Outcomes were measured within 6 months of index date. Healthcare utilization included encounters, procedures, radiology, lab tests, and medications. Results Among 2810 cancer and 11,240 non‐cancer patients, all evaluated healthcare utilization measures were significantly more common in cancer patients. The largest relative differences were observed for long inpatient stay (risk ratio [RR] 26.32, 95% confidence interval [CI] 15.00–46.17), computed tomography (RR 23.59, 95% CI 19.24–28.92), blood culture (RR 37.04, 95% CI 9.58–143.14), and intravenous medication (RR 17.69, 95% CI 8.75–35.75). Death within 6 months was higher for cancer versus non‐cancer patients (RR 38.37, 95% CI 12.91–114.04). Conclusions Using the OMOP CDM, we found greater healthcare utilization and worse clinical outcomes among pediatric cancer patients than non‐cancer patients, with the largest relative differences observed for inpatient stay, computed tomography, blood culture, and intravenous medication. These findings provide insight into resource utilization patterns and illustrate the OMOP CDM research potential for multicenter studies.

papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Background Around 90% of children with cancer live in low‐ and middle‐income countries (LMICs), with the majority dying of their disease. Despite the need for quality end‐of‐life (EoL) care in LMICs, access and integration remain limited. Quality indicators (QIs) can assess and provide standards for high‐quality care. The aim of this study was to develop QIs for EoL care for children diagnosed with cancer in LMICs. Methods The QIs were identified and prioritized through a multi‐phase process: (1) literature review identified potential QIs from existing guidelines, standards, and published studies; (2) modified Delphi approach engaged global experts to assess the importance and feasibility of QIs; and (3) prioritization conducted using a Discrete Choice Experiment (DCE) with experts and dot voting prioritization exercise with bereaved family members. Results From the literature review, 73 potential QIs were identified. Fifty‐six global experts from 27 countries participated in the modified Delphi. Sixty‐four indicators across seven domains were deemed important with 25 identified as both important and feasible. Forty‐one global experts from 23 countries participated in the DCE prioritization and 12 bereaved family members from nine countries participated in the dot voting prioritization. While experts and family members prioritized some indicators similarly (i.e., symptom management), family members placed higher priority on QIs addressing communication and anticipatory guidance. Conclusion This study describes a robust, context‐specific process which identified QIs for pediatric EoL care in LMICs. Future efforts will pilot and refine the QIs to demonstrate feasibility, sustainability, and impact on care quality. Precis This study assessed potential quality indicators (QIs) for pediatric end‐of‐life (EoL) care in low‐ and middle‐income countries (LMICs) through a multi‐phase process involving global experts and bereaved families. The findings provide a set of potential QIs to evaluate and improve EoL care for children with cancer in LMICs.

papers.abstract: Experimental oncofertility remains fragmented across models of cancer biology, treatment-associated gonadotoxicity, fertility preservation, and reproductive recovery. We propose extending the Oncopig concept into a translational platform that reconnects these states within one genetically defined, cancer-bearing host. The Oncopig provides the oncologic backbone, combining programmable cancer in an immunocompetent large-animal host with clinically scaled intervention and longitudinal sampling. High-resolution porcine genomics, CRISPR-based genome engineering, somatic-cell nuclear transfer for line generation, comparative experimental pathology, and mature reproductive biotechnology extend this architecture toward reproductive endpoints. Here, programmability refers to deliberate specification of the cancer state-genotype, cell lineage or induction strategy, and timing-whereas the reproductive phenotype is measured longitudinally rather than programmed. Distant-cancer modules can test whether cancer status modifies gonadotoxicity, while reproductive-organ modules require disease-specific alleles, appropriate cell-of-origin targeting, and pathology-led validation. Because porcine and human reproduction align in several endocrine and gonadal processes but differ in cycle organization, implantation, placentation, and pregnancy, translation should emphasize process-level endpoints rather than numerical equivalence. The platform is particularly suited to unresolved questions involving targeted therapies and immunotherapies, preservation timing, and pediatric or prepubertal patients. Porcine reproductive biotechnology provides functional endpoints from gonadal tissue and gametes to embryos and offspring. Rather than replacing rodent or human-based models, the Oncopig framework adds an integrated translational layer for questions requiring clinically scaled intervention, longitudinal physiology, and functional reproductive recovery.

papers.abstract: This study assessed MAGEA4 expression in recurrent bladder cancer, examined its relationships with molecular and immune subtypes, and evaluated its association with treatment response and prognosis. This single-center exploratory cohort study enrolled 20 patients. RNA sequencing was performed on recurrent tumor tissue samples. The EU molecular subtypes were determined. Immune subtypes were classified, and PD-L1 and HER2 status were assessed. GO, KEGG, and Reactome enrichment analyses were performed. Patients were divided into MAGEA4-high and MAGEA4-low groups using the cohort median expression level. Differences in the composition of molecular/immune subtypes were compared. Within-cohort ROC analysis was used to assess discrimination of clinical benefit, and PFS was analyzed using Kaplan-Meier and Cox methods. The top 20 genes with the most prominent between-subtype expression differences were identified. Genes upregulated in the Luminal papillary subtype were enriched in terms related to cell-cell junctions and epithelial structure maintenance. Downregulated genes were enriched in pathways associated with immune activation and inflammatory infiltration. Enrichment signals involved the PI3K-Akt, MAPK, neuroactive ligand-receptor interaction, and JAK-STAT pathways. Significant differences in PD-L1 status, TMIT subtypes, and EU subtypes were observed between MAGEA4-high and MAGEA4-low groups, and the six MAGEA4-immune/molecular association tests remained below q<0.05 after Benjamini-Hochberg correction. MAGEA4 expression also differed according to PD-L1 status, TMIT subtype, and binary EU subtype grouping. Within-cohort ROC analysis yielded AUC values of 0.798, 0.800, and 0.750 in the overall, immunotherapy, and combination-therapy cohorts, respectively; the bootstrap optimism-corrected overall AUC was 0.793. High MAGEA4 expression was associated with shorter PFS. MAGEA4 expression was associated with PD-L1 status, TMIT immune subtypes, and EU molecular subtypes, showed within-cohort discrimination of clinical benefit, and was associated with poorer PFS. These findings support further evaluation of MAGEA4 as a candidate molecular stratification marker in independent cohorts.

papers.abstract: Platinum-based chemotherapy plus cytoreductive surgery represents the standard first-line therapy for ovarian cancer (OC), which yields robust early therapeutic responses in most patients. However, platinum resistance is a formidable clinical hurdle, and how macrophages mediate drug resistance within the OC tumor microenvironment remains poorly understood. We cultured SKOV3 OC cells and THP-1 monocytes, induced THP-1 differentiation into M2d tumor-associated macrophages. Stable apolipoprotein E (ApoE) -overexpressing SKOV3 cell lines were constructed via lentiviral transfection and puromycin screening. We established nude mouse subcutaneous xenograft models with mixed tumor cells and M2d macrophages, administered cisplatin treatment and collected tumor tissues after sacrifice by cervical dislocation. RNA was extracted from tumor samples to conduct RT-qPCR for gene expression detection. Tumor tissue sections were prepared for HE staining, TUNEL apoptosis staining, and Western blot analysis to detect ApoE and phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K)/AKT/mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) pathway protein expression. Using nude mouse subcutaneous xenograft models, we demonstrated that M2d-type tumor-associated macrophages (M2d TAMs) promote platinum resistance and elevate tumoral ApoE levels. In OC xenografts with stable ApoE overexpression, cisplatin-induced apoptosis was profoundly repressed, resulting in reduced cisplatin sensitivity, while this inhibitory effect was not observed in the empty vector control group. Mechanistically, ApoE activates the PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling cascade to counteract cisplatin cytotoxicity by suppressing cell death and sustaining pro-survival signals. Overall, this study reveals that M2d TAMs induce platinum resistance in OC cells via exosomes carrying ApoE.

papers.abstract: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) are associated with a wide spectrum of immune-related adverse events (irAEs), reflecting enhanced immune activation. Pancreatic involvement is rare and typically presents as asymptomatic hyperlipasemia or diffuse inflammatory changes. Focal or multifocal mass-like presentations are uncommon and may mimic pancreatic malignancy, posing a significant diagnostic challenge. We report the case of a 48-year-old woman treated with Pembrolizumab and Paclitaxel for axillary recurrence of triple-negative breast cancer. After four cycles, FDG PET/CT demonstrated a complete metabolic response at the initial tumor site but revealed new multifocal hypermetabolic pancreatic lesions. Magnetic resonance imaging confirmed multiple pancreatic masses, raising suspicion of metastatic disease or dissociated response. Endoscopic ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration at two concordant pancreatic sites showed neutrophil-predominant inflammatory infiltration without malignant cells, consistent with immune-related pancreatic injury. The patient subsequently developed symptoms of exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, which improved after concomitant initiation of pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy and corticosteroid tapering, with the relative contribution of each not clearly distinguishable. Follow-up imaging demonstrated complete resolution of pancreatic lesions. This case highlights a rare mass-forming (pseudotumoral) phenotype of ICI-related pancreatic injury (ICI-PI), presenting as multifocal FDG-avid pancreatic pseudomasses. Such findings may represent a major pitfall in PET/CT interpretation under immunotherapy, particularly in the context of otherwise favorable oncologic response. Histopathological confirmation is critical to distinguish immune-mediated inflammation from metastatic disease. This observation supports the concept of organ-specific immune dysregulation driven by ICIs and expands the radiological spectrum of pancreatic irAEs. Multifocal FDG-avid pancreatic lesions occurring during immunotherapy should raise suspicion for immune-related pancreatic injury (ICI-PI), especially in the absence of systemic progression. Early recognition is essential to avoid misdiagnosis and inappropriate treatment decisions.

papers.abstract: Successful cancer immunotherapy requires not only tumor cell killing but also the activation of innate and adaptive immune responses. The inhibitor of apoptosis (IAP) proteins cIAP1, cIAP2 and XIAP act as key suppressors of RIPK1-driven immunogenic cell death, thereby enabling tumor immune evasion and limiting the effectiveness of immune checkpoint blockade (ICB). ASTX660 (tolinapant) is a non-peptidomimetic antagonist with a balanced activity against all clinically relevant IAPs, designed to lower the TNF cytotoxicity threshold and sensitize tumors to T cell-mediated killing. Here, we present results from the phase I ASTEROID trial (NCT05082259), evaluating ASTX660 in combination with pembrolizumab in patients with advanced solid tumors. Primary endpoints were recommended phase 2 dose (RP2D) and safety, while secondary endpoints were anti-tumor activity and pharmacokinetics. The combination was well tolerated and demonstrated early evidence of efficacy. RP2D was ASTX660 150 mg (7-days-on/14-days-off) with pembrolizumab. Overall response rate was 33%, including responses in ER⁺ breast cancers typically resistant to ICB. Integrated translational analyses reveal that response is associated with a TNF/IFN-enriched inflammatory tumor microenvironment, increased tumor antigenicity and enhanced TCR clonal diversity, whereas resistance correlates with a CCR4/6/7/8-driven TAM/Treg-dominant niche. Together, these results provide clinical proof-of-concept that dual IAP and PD-1 blockade sensitize tumors, while identifying candidate biomarkers to guide patient stratification in future studies.

papers.abstract: During the early phases of oncogenic clonal expansion, precancerous cells experience replication stress that threatens both genomic integrity and viability. How replication stress tolerance (RST) mechanisms are dynamically reprogrammed across the different stages of cancer progression remains elusive. Here, we identify PrimPol as a central regulator that executes two fundamentally distinct RST modes in response to oncogenic KRAS-induced heterochromatin-associated replication stress (K-HaRS). Unexpectedly, during acute K-HaRS, an unphosphorylated form of PrimPol cooperates with the fork remodeler SMARCAL1 to actively slow fork progression, stabilizing challenged forks and limiting engagement of error-prone DNA synthesis. As K-HaRS persists, PrimPol undergoes an ATR-dependent functional switch, whereby its phosphorylated form promotes repriming while fork slowing is attenuated, enabling replication to proceed across heterochromatin barriers despite persistent stress. Strikingly, loss of PrimPol enforces chronic reliance on the error-prone Rev1-Polζ-dependent synthesis and compromises cellular fitness under KRAS-driven stress. Thus, these findings establish PrimPol as a context-dependent regulator of RST that, through ATR-dependent toggling of its functional modes, coordinates fork slowing and repriming to safeguard replication fork stability while permitting an optimal compromise of genome stability that would fuel oncogenic clonal evolution.

papers.abstract: Oral mucositis (OM) is a major toxicity in patients with head and neck cancer undergoing radiotherapy. Here we conducted a double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomized phase II trial (NCT06285591) from March 2024 to January 2025 at West China Hospital of Sichuan University to evaluate whether Limosilactobacillus reuteri (L. reuteri) supplementation could reduce severe OM (SOM; WHO Oral Toxicity criteria grade ≥3). A total of 160 patients were randomly assigned to receive L. reuteri probiotic lozenges or placebo twice daily during radiotherapy. The primary endpoint was the incidence of SOM, and secondary endpoints included SOM onset and duration, as well as the incidence, onset, and duration of any-grade OM. Safety outcomes were monitored throughout the study. The primary endpoint was met, with a lower incidence of SOM in the L. reuteri group than in the placebo group (37.5% vs 61.3%; relative risk 0.61; 95% confidence interval 0.44-0.85; absolute risk reduction 23.8 percentage points, 95% CI 8.7% to 38.8%; P = 0.004). L. reuteri supplementation also delayed SOM onset and shortened SOM duration. No significant safety concerns were observed. These findings indicate that L. reuteri supplementation reduces SOM incidence and severity in patients with head and neck cancer receiving radiotherapy.

papers.abstract: Most pediatric acute myeloid leukemia (pAML) patients achieve complete remission after chemotherapy, yet nearly 40% ultimately relapse and die from their disease. High risk cases are typically referred for stem cell transplantation (SCT) in first remission, but because SCT is associated with substantial toxicity and cures after relapse are rare, accurate risk prediction is critical. Here, we show that combining the detection of chemoresistant cell populations, inferred from single-cell transcriptomic profiles of paired diagnosis-relapse samples, and cytogenetic biomarkers at diagnosis with measurable residual disease after induction chemotherapy, substantially improves risk prediction. This approach identifies a patient subgroup comprising 20% of the patients who do not undergo SCT, with a 5-year event-free survival below 40%, and accounting for nearly half of all deaths in this population. Molecular characterization of these cell populations reveals therapeutic vulnerabilities and potential targeted treatment strategies for high-risk pAML, providing a framework for precision oncology diagnosis and intervention.

papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Metastasis of malignant tumors arising from epithelial organs to sentinel lymph nodes has important implications for prognosis, staging, and therapeutic decision‐making. Recent insights into anatomic pathways, pathogenesis, molecular interactions, and genetic factors have encouraged scientists and clinicians to develop drugs that target mechanisms of lymph node metastasis. We summarize important aspects of the vast literature that pertains to these mechanisms, focusing on five phases that implicate invasion through the epithelial basement membrane and tumor microenvironment, into initial lymphatics, and, after flow through lymphatic trunks, into the sentinel lymph node. Valuable information regarding tumor cell‐directed motility, lymphangiogenesis, host cells that enhance metastasis, immune responses to tumor antigens, and tumor‐induced changes in sentinel lymph node(s) provides a promising avenue for the continued development of new therapeutic approaches to prevent and treat metastasis. This article reviews these aspects by synthesizing current scientific and clinical advances and translating them for medical professionals.

papers.abstract: Alternative polyadenylation (APA) is a pervasive post-transcriptional regulatory mechanism that generates transcript isoforms with distinct 3' untranslated regions, terminal exons, or coding potential, thereby influencing mRNA stability, translation, localization, and protein output. Rather than representing a uniform 3'UTR-shortening process, APA comprises heterogeneous 3'-end regulatory events, including tandem 3'UTR APA and upstream APA events such as intronic polyadenylation (IPA), which differ in mechanisms, detection strategies, functional consequences, and clinical interpretation. Dysregulated APA is increasingly recognized as an important contributor to cancer initiation and progression. Tandem 3'UTR APA can remove miRNA- or RNA-binding protein-mediated repression and enhance oncogenic transcript output, whereas upstream APA events, including IPA, can generate prematurely terminated RNAs, truncated proteins, soluble isoforms, or neoantigenic products. In this review, we summarize the classification and biological consequences of major APA events, as well as experimental and computational approaches for APA analysis. We then discuss regulatory mechanisms involving core 3'-end processing factors, RNA-binding proteins, splicing-polyadenylation coupling in upstream APA/IPA, transcription-associated regulation, and promoter-terminator communication. Functionally, aberrant APA contributes to proliferation, invasion and metastasis, metabolic reprogramming, tumor microenvironment remodeling, antitumor immunity, and immune escape. Finally, we highlight APA events, APA regulators, 3'UTR-based signatures, and upstream APA/IPA-derived products as emerging biomarkers and discuss small-molecule, RNA-based, and CRISPR-based strategies for targeting APA or 3'-end processing in cancer.

papers.abstract: Initially characterized as an epigenetic marker for transcriptional regulation, lysine lactylation is now recognized as a pervasive posttranslational modification with extensive functions beyond those associated with chromatin. Recent methodological advances in the resolution of stereoisomeric dynamics have established L-lactylation as the predominant glycolysis-derived functional form, providing a metabolic switch that couples glycolytic flux to oncogenic signaling. Here, we provide a comprehensive overview of non-histone L-lactylation in cancer biology. We define the spatially compartmentalized catalytic network governing this process, detailing how nuclear EP300/CBP, cytosolic AARS1, and mitochondrial AARS2 mediate stereospecific targeted modifications. At the molecular level, non-histone L-lactylation alters protein biophysics via charge neutralization, steric hindrance, and interface remodeling. These physicochemical alterations govern fundamental enzymatic kinetics, complex assembly, subcellular trafficking, and proteasomal degradation processes. Through primarily transcription-independent mechanisms, L-lactylation enables cancer cells to sustain metabolic flexibility, promote the repair of damaged DNA, and foster an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment. Because tumors exploit these regulatory networks to drive adaptive resistance across diverse therapeutic modalities, we examine current strategies for pharmacological intervention. Finally, we highlight critical unresolved questions in this field. Notably, the identification of lactylation-specific readers and the development of stereoisomer-resolved chemobiological tools will be essential to fully leverage this metabolism-modification axis for cancer therapy.

papers.abstract: Neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy is a standard treatment for locally advanced rectal cancer, yet acquired resistance limits durable tumor control. Whether stress-adaptive acetyl-group metabolism contributes to this resistance remains unclear. We performed a genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 loss-of-function screen under fractionated irradiation and integrated the results with transcriptomic and proteomic profiling of radioresistant colorectal cancer models established by stepwise irradiation. CRAT function was interrogated using genetic perturbation, catalytic-dead reconstitution, acetylation-mimetic p65 rescue, RELA depletion, stable-isotope tracing, free coenzyme A quantification, NF-κB reporter assays, chromatin immunoprecipitation-qPCR, and xenograft and syngeneic tumor models. CRAT was prioritized through cross-platform convergence of the CRISPR screen with transcriptomic and proteomic signatures of radioresistant cells, and post-treatment tumors with poorer pathological regression showed higher CRAT and nuclear p65 immunohistochemical scores. CRAT manipulation had limited, model-dependent effects on basal proliferation but more pronounced effects after irradiation, where CRAT loss reduced clonogenic survival and was associated with increased oxidative stress and persistent DNA damage. Stable-isotope tracing showed that irradiation increased acetate-to-acetylcarnitine flux and expanded the free coenzyme A pool in control cells, whereas CRAT loss disrupted this acetyl-group buffering. Mechanistically, CRAT catalytic activity helped maintain irradiation-induced p65 Lys310 acetylation, H3K27ac enrichment at NF-κB-responsive loci, and NF-κB-associated transcriptional output through a p300/CBP-sensitive acetylation axis. p65-K310Q rescue and RELA depletion supported p65 acetylation and RELA-dependent transcription as downstream contributors to, rather than sole mediators of, CRAT-dependent radioprotection. In syngeneic MC38 tumors, Crat deletion enhanced the response to fractionated radiotherapy. These findings support CRAT-dependent acetyl-group metabolism as a contributor to an NF-κB-associated radioprotective program and nominate this metabolic dependency as a candidate vulnerability for radiosensitization in colorectal cancer.

papers.abstract: To evaluate the prospective risk of high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion or worse (HSIL+) in high-risk HPV (HR-HPV)positive women, assessing the independent and interactive effects of baseline HPV16-status, genotype multiplicity, and follow-up HPV persistence. A prospective cohort of 2562 HR-HPV-positive women referred for colposcopy were categorized into four groups: single non-HPV16, single HPV16, HPV16 plus other HR types, or multiple non-HPV16. HSIL+ risk was analysed using Cox-proportional-hazards-regression, restricted mean survival time (RMST) at 36months, and Fine-Gray competing-risk models. Multivariable logistic regression evaluated concurrent HSIL+ risk associated with follow-up HPV persistence. Overall, 691 women (27.0%) developed HSIL+. Infection with HPV16 plus other HR types carried the highest risk (adjusted hazard ratio [aHR]2.10, 95%CI: 1.69-2.62) and shorter median HSIL+-free survival than single non-HPV16 infection (24 vs. 54months), corresponding to 5.1 fewer HSIL+-free-months at 36months (p<0.001). Baseline HPV16 positivity and genotype multiplicity exerted independent, additive effects without multiplicative interaction (adjusted p=0.600). Incorporating multiplicity improved model discrimination beyond entry cytology and HPV16 status (concordance index 0.612 vs. 0.587, p<0.001). Results remained robust in competing-risk analyses (subdistribution HR2.03, 95%CI: 1.64-2.52) and after excluding early-treated women (aHR2.00, 95%CI: 1.52-2.62). Follow-up viral persistence strongly correlated with concurrent HSIL+ (aHR5.71-8.59, p<0.001), reflecting a cross-sectional risk correlation complementary to baseline prognostication. Baseline HPV16 positivity and genotype multiplicity are independent, additive risk factors for HSIL+, with HPV16 plus other HR types marking the highest-risk subgroup. Genotype multiplicity provides distinct clinical predictive value alongside HPV16 status, while follow-up HPV persistence offers complementary, non-redundant information for concurrent risk evaluation in risk-based management strategies.

papers.abstract: Activated Cdc42-associated kinase 1 (ACK1; encoded by the TNK2 gene) is an oncogenic protein of the non-receptor tyrosine kinase family and functions downstream of RAS and activated transmembrane receptor tyrosine kinases such as EGFR. Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), which constitutes around 85% of lung cancer cases, often exhibits amplification or overexpression of the TNK2 gene. This study focuses on demonstrating the therapeutic potential of targeting ACK1 for the treatment of NSCLC. The small molecule ACK1 inhibitor, (R)-9b, preferentially inhibited the growth of NSCLC cell lines possessing activated ACK1, which often have RAS mutations. (R)-9b induced G2/M arrest and robust cellular senescence primarily in the sensitive RAS mutant NSCLC cell lines; these effects were confirmed with ACK1 knockdown. (R)-9b significantly inhibited the growth of both cell line-derived and patient-derived NSCLC xenografts with RAS mutations in vivo. Mechanistically, ACK1 inhibition suppresses topoisomerase 2A (Topo IIα; encoded by TOP2A) expression, along with downregulation of the expression of gene sets associated with the regulation of DNA repair and replication, resulting in accumulation of DNA damage and subsequent cellular senescence. Overall, RAS mutation in NSCLC cell lines activates the Cdc42/ACK1 axis, conferring sensitivity to ACK1 inhibition that causes accumulation of DNA damage via inhibition of Topo IIα and DNA repair, G2/M arrest, and eventual cellular senescence in RAS mutant NSCLC cells.

papers.abstract: The IL-36γ/IL-36R signaling axis mediates cellular communication in various contexts and has recently been implicated in pro-fibrotic responses. However, its specific role in oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC), which is characterized by abundant cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs), remains elusive. Here, we investigated the contribution of IL-36γ/IL-36R signaling to CAF function and OSCC progression. Immunohistochemical analysis of patient samples revealed that IL-36γ was highly expressed in CAFs and that higher co-expression of IL-36γ/IL-36R in CAFs was associated with more invasive patterns and shorter disease-free survival. By integrating tumor cell lines with patient-derived organoids (PDOs), we established three co-culture systems to model these interactions. These models revealed that IL-36γ signaling enhanced CAF proliferation and extracellular matrix remodeling. Mechanistically, the IL-36γ/IL-36R axis in CAFs increased ERK1/2-dependent CCL20 secretion, which in turn promoted tumor cell invasion. Pharmacological blockade of IL-36R attenuated both the IL-36γ-induced increase in CAF abundance and the associated pro-tumorigenic CAF phenotypes in vivo. Collectively, these findings suggest that the IL-36γ/IL-36R-ERK1/2-CCL20 signaling cascade participates in CAF-tumor interactions. Targeting IL-36R may therefore represent a promising therapeutic strategy for invasive OSCC.

papers.abstract: Abstract Background Edematous malnutrition, aka kwashiorkor, is a phenotype of severe malnutrition whose pathophysiology remains poorly understood. Methods In this case-control study, we employed plasma lipidomics, metabolomics, and proteomics, urine metabolomics and gut microbiome profiling to delineate molecular features specific to kwashiorkor in 60 children aged 6–59 months from Niger compared to marasmus ( n = 60) and non-malnourished children (NAM) ( n = 60) matched by age, sex, and clinical triage score. Features were defined as kwashiorkor-specific if they also correlated with edema severity and normalized following nutritional rehabilitation. Results We identified a plasma proteomic factor featuring lumican, gelsolin, and tetranectin and a lipidomic factor enriched in sphingolipids. Both differed in kwashiorkor compared to marasmus and NAM, were associated with edema grade, and trended towards normalcy after nutritional treatment, which are consistent with ECM remodeling and sphingolipid dysregulation. In contrast, neither (plasma and urine) metabolomic profiles nor gut microbiome composition showed kwashiorkor-specific signatures, although our urine and gut microbiome analyses may be underpowered. Conclusion These findings advance understanding of kwashiorkor pathophysiology beyond nutrient deficiency and highlight ECM and sphingolipid features associated with its distinct clinical and molecular characteristics compared to marasmus.

papers.abstract: Timdarpacept (IMM01) is a recombinant signal regulatory protein α-IgG1 fusion protein that exerts antitumor activity by blocking the "don't eat me" signal while simultaneously activating the "eat me" signal, inducing robust antibody-dependent cellular phagocytosis. We report the final phase II results of treatment-naïve higher risk chronic myelomonocytic leukemia (CMML) patients treated with IMM01 in combination with azacitidine. We assessed the safety and efficacy of IMM01 in combination with azacitidine (AZA) as first-line therapy for newly diagnosed CMML patients. IMM01 was administered intravenously at 2.0 mg/kg weekly, and AZA was administered subcutaneously at 75 mg/m² on days 1-7 of each 28-day cycle. As of the data cut-off on May 13, 2025, 24 patients were enrolled. Of 22 efficacy-evaluable patients, the overall response rate (ORR) was 72.7% (16/22; 95% CI 49.8-89.3), including 27.3% complete response (CR), 13.6% marrow CR (mCR) with hematologic improvement (HI), 4.5% HI alone, and 27.3% mCR alone. The median time to response was 1.8 months (range, 0.9-3.6), and the median duration of response was 16.9 months (95% CI 5.1-NE). Median overall survival and progression-free survival were 22.2 months (95% CI 9.0-NE) and 17.8 months (95% CI 5.3-NE), respectively. The most common grade ≥ 3 treatment-related adverse events (≥ 10%) were lymphopenia (66.7%), leukopenia (62.5%), neutropenia (62.5%), thrombocytopenia (58.3%), anemia (33.3%), and pneumonia (16.7%). IMM01 in combination with AZA was generally well tolerated and effective in treatment-naïve higher risk CMML patients. Trial registration ClinicalTrials.gov identiﬁer: NCT05140811.

papers.abstract: Familial hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (FHLH) is classically pediatric, but adult-onset disease is increasingly recognized. Whether adult-onset FHLH differs from pediatric/adolescent-onset disease remains incompletely defined. We aimed to characterize age-related differences in a nationwide multicenter cohort of patients with FHLH in China. We conducted a nationwide multicenter retrospective study of 223 patients with FHLH from 27 centers in China. Genetic architecture, central nervous system (CNS) involvement, allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (allo-HSCT), and survival were compared by age at onset, with adult-onset disease defined as onset at age ≥ 18 years and pediatric/adolescent-onset disease as onset at < 18 years. In this cohort, adult-onset disease accounted for 54/223 cases (24.2%). In the PRF1/UNC13D subset (n = 192), higher non-truncating variant burden was associated with adult onset (unadjusted OR per additional recorded variant, 1.95; 95% CI, 1.17-3.39), although the association attenuated after adjustment for gene and zygosity (adjusted OR, 1.58; 95% CI, 0.94-2.75). Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) was the predominant documented trigger in adults. CNS involvement was common across age groups (46.4%), with uncertain prognostic significance. Adults underwent allo-HSCT less frequently (49.1% vs. 70.2%) and were less often in complete response before transplantation (15.4% vs. 46.8%). Adult onset remained associated with poorer overall survival after multivariable adjustment including time-dependent allo-HSCT (HR, 3.74; 95% CI, 1.96-7.12). Post-HSCT survival was also poorer in adults. Adult-onset FHLH was associated with non-truncating variant enrichment and poorer overall and post-HSCT survival. These findings support considering inherited disease despite acquired triggers and careful assessment of disease control and transplant-related risks in adults with FHLH.

papers.abstract: Targeted protein degradation (TPD) has significantly influenced cancer therapy by enabling the targeting of traditionally undruggable oncogenic drivers such as transcription factors, chromatin remodelers, and mediators of protein-protein interactions, overcoming limitations of conventional inhibitors. This approach harnesses endogenous cellular machinery, specifically the ubiquitin-proteasome system and lysosomal pathways, to achieve precise and efficient elimination of pathogenic proteins. Currently, one degradation-based agent, vepdegestrant, has been approved by FDA, while most agents remain in Phase I or II evaluation, representing significant progress in addressing previously intractable targets in cancers. Nevertheless, a substantial number of disease-relevant proteins remain challenging to modulate effectively. This review focuses on undruggable targets in cancer and distinguishes three target categories: 1) Structurally undruggable targets; 2) Formerly undruggable, now inhibitor-accessible but degradation offers a mechanistic advantage; 3) Non-enzymatic targets. We highlight recent advances in the development of TPD strategies against these elusive targets to a cutoff of 30 September 2026, with the aim of providing a more systematic theoretical foundation for the broader application of the developing TPD in cancer therapeutics.

papers.abstract: While the association between gut microbiota and cholangiocarcinoma (CCA) has been explored, existing research has been limited to bacterial components. The alterations in non-bacterial members (fungi, archaea, and viruses) and their functional characteristics in CCA remain unclear. This study aimed to comprehensively characterize the multi-kingdom gut microbiota and functional profiles in CCA patients and develop a non-invasive diagnostic model. We performed metagenomic sequencing on 700 fecal samples collected from three distinct regions in China, comprising 289 CCA patients, 312 healthy controls, and 99 hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) patients. Multi-kingdom microbial composition and functional profiles were analyzed. We integrated multiple machine learning algorithms to generate 117 distinct modeling schemes for constructing and screening the optimal CCA diagnostic model. The model was validated across three independent cohorts and tested for specificity against HCC. We also benchmarked the model against established diagnostic approaches by reviewing 15 CCA clinical practice guidelines/consensus statements and their cited evidence and by evaluating model detection in CA19-9-positive and CA19-9-negative patients. Extensive alterations were identified in CCA patients across multi-kingdom and functional layers, including 198 archaeal, 154 bacterial, 78 fungal, and 120 viral species, as well as 278 genes, 99 pathways, and 151 carbohydrate-active enzymes (CAZymes). A panel of 21 multi-kingdom and functional markers demonstrated superior diagnostic accuracy with an average AUC of 91% across three validation cohorts, outperforming any single-kingdom model. The model exhibited high specificity in distinguishing CCA from HCC, achieving an AUC of 99.74% with a false positive rate of 11.11%. Benchmarking supported a complementary role as a noninvasive screening aid, the model showed pooled sensitivity and specificity of 96.2%, and 78.5%, respectively, and detected 97.6% of CA19-9-negative CCA cases. This study represents the first comprehensive characterization of multi-kingdom gut microbiome and functional markers in cholangiocarcinoma. Gut multi-kingdom and functional microbial signatures represent a promising noninvasive tool that may aid the screening and early identification of cholangiocarcinoma in high-risk populations, complementing existing diagnostic approaches.

papers.abstract: Analysis of cell-free DNA (cfDNA) methylation can enable noninvasive disease detection by leveraging tissue-specific epigenetic differences between malignant and nonmalignant cells. However, such analyses can be confounded by the repair of jagged DNA fragment ends during double-stranded sequencing library preparation, which introduces spurious methylation signals into cfDNA molecules. Here we present JEEPERS, a framework to detect and correct jagged-end-induced methylation errors while preserving duplex integrity and native methylation patterns. We showed high fidelity for measuring tumor burden and demonstrated allele-specific methylation differences at recurrent somatic mutations, revealing a link between adjacent CpG methylation and EGFR/TP53 driver and resistance mutations. We further demonstrated enhanced diagnostic performance across liquid biopsy applications, including tumor-type-specific methylation profiles, hemimethylation profiling, epigenetic-clock-based age estimation and cell type deconvolution. By faithfully correcting end-repair errors, JEEPERS provides a versatile framework for integrating mutations and methylation features in cfDNA at high resolution, enabling more precise molecular profiling and disease monitoring.

papers.abstract: Abstract The hyperactive kinase FLT3-ITD causes acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and is a prognostic biomarker. We synthesized and characterized MA191 as a novel von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) E3 ubiquitin ligase-based proteolysis targeting chimera (PROTAC) for FLT3. MA191 induces apoptosis in cultured and primary AML patient cells harboring FLT3-ITD (IC 50 =9.6-11 nM; EC 50 =0.001-0.883 µM). Comparison with a VHL-binding-deficient stereoisomer of MA191 demonstrates that FLT3-ITD degradation is superior to kinase inhibition ( p < 0.03). Rapid depletion of FLT3-ITD by MA191 (DC 50 =10 nM) requires VHL, neddylation, proteasome activity, and the pro-apoptotic BH3-only protein BIM. MA191 reduces FLT3-ITD prior to apoptosis, uncovering apoptosis-independent roles of BIM for protein stability. Higher expression levels of FLT3 in leukemia cells than in healthy cells ( n = 3675/ n = 1249) are associated with worse AML patient survival ( p = 0.0099). MA191 does not harm healthy blood and bone marrow progenitor cells or myeloid cell differentiation. In Danio rerio larvae, MA191 halts AML cell proliferation without significant toxicity. Human stromal cell interactions and mutations in the tyrosine kinase domain of FLT3-ITD that confer resistance to FLT3 inhibitors do not abolish anti-leukemic effects of MA191. Accordingly, leukemia cells with acquired resistance to MA191 lack such mutations. We offer a framework for fast-acting next-generation FLT3 degraders that overcome resistance mechanisms to classical inhibitors.

papers.abstract: To elucidate the mechanisms underlying therapy-induced resistance, we investigated the temporal dynamics of the polyploid giant cancer cell (PGCC) life cycle following treatment with the microtubule-destabilizing agent vincristine (VCR). Longitudinal live-cell fluorescence imaging revealed that VCR-induced mitotic suppression activated a distinct PGCC life cycle characterized by nuclear amplification and progressive cellular reprogramming. At the cellular level, PGCCs entered a senescence-like state accompanied by an enhanced senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP), increased epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT), acquisition of early embryonic-like features, and multilineage differentiation potential into ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm. PGCC-derived progeny exhibited dose- and time-dependent changes in proliferative behavior, aggressive phenotypes in vitro, along with time-dependent tumorigenic potential in vivo. Remarkably, at the tissue level, PGCCs also underwent spatial nuclear reorganization and self-organization into morphologically defined glandular epithelial structures exhibiting varying degrees of tissue maturation, reminiscent of early embryonic development. Silencing IL1β, IL6, or IL8, or pharmacologically inhibiting their receptors, suppressed PGCC formation, budding, EMT, and embryonic-like reprogramming associated with tissue morphogenesis. Furthermore, NAMPT emerged as a key regulator of embryonic-like stemness, glandular morphogenesis, and structural expansion. Together, these findings reveal that therapeutic stress activates a PGCC life cycle capable of generating two divergent outcomes: resistant tumor regeneration through clonal selection of undifferentiated tumor cells and organized tissue differentiation through spatial nuclear reprogramming. Our study establishes a conceptual framework linking therapy-induced polyploidization, developmental plasticity, and resistance generation at both cellular and tissue levels.

papers.abstract: The bone marrow microenvironment (BME) has a significant effect on bortezomib (BTZ)-based chemotherapy in patients with multiple myeloma (MM). However, how BME components drive effective BTZ-based chemotherapy to facilitate antitumor responses has yet to be fully understood. Using single-cell transcriptome analysis, we discerned a notable increase in the density of tumor-associated IL1B+ monocytes (TAMO_IL1B), a CD14+ monocyte subcluster, within the optimal responders (OR) group compared with the suboptimal responders (SOR) group. TAMO_IL1B in the OR group had significantly greater effects on the TGF-β signaling pathway. The ligand-receptor pair (THBS1-SDC1) interaction intensity in the THBS1 signaling pathway between TAMO_IL1B and tumor plasma cells (TPC) in the OR group was significantly greater than that in the SOR group. Furthermore, pseudotime trajectory analysis indicated that TAMO_IL1B predominantly occupied late differentiation stages and was associated with a favorable response within the OR group. These findings reveal a previously unrecognized role for TAMO_IL1B in shaping antitumor immunity. The THBS1-SDC1 axis may contribute to interactions between monocytes and plasma cells; however, functional validation is required before any therapeutic implications can be drawn.

papers.abstract: The immune checkpoints and their inhibitors are revolutionary advances in tumour immunotherapy. Immune checkpoints, however, have a broad spectrum effect. They not only contribute to tumour immune escape, but also are involved in the regulation of the pathopathological processes of numerous inflammatory illnesses, such as sepsis, autoimmune diseases, organ transplant rejection, and viral infections, among others. Today, a considerable gap in knowledge remains regarding immune checkpoints and immune checkpoint inhibitors in non-tumour inflammatory diseases, which remains largely unaddressed. At the same time, the emergence of immune-related adverse events and resistance challenges related to the clinical use of immune checkpoint inhibitors is becoming increasingly prominent, posing a significant obstacle to their application across various diseases. To overcome such issues, this narrative review establishes a systematic framework that links immune checkpoints to various inflammatory diseases and explores the associated therapeutic and clinical challenges. These diseases pose therapeutic and clinical challenges of immune checkpoint inhibitors, which we explore. The paper not only thoroughly describes the clinical picture, pathophysiology, and interventions in immunologic adverse events but also suggests a prospective strategy to confront the existing problems with immune checkpoint inhibitors in 3 dimensions: evaluation, management, and prevention. It will attempt to present a new conceptual framework for a comprehensive understanding of the dual role of immune checkpoints (in maintaining immune homeostasis and facilitating disease progression) and to provide a solid theoretical foundation for the development of safer and more effective cross-disease immunotherapy.

papers.abstract: Abstract Background T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL) is an aggressive malignancy with poor prognosis, especially in relapsed/refractory patients. Aberrant PI3K/AKT/mTOR and NOTCH1 signaling converge on c-MYC to drive proliferation and ribosome biogenesis, but single-agent inhibitors targeting these pathways have shown limited clinical efficacy. Methods An FDA-approved drug library screen identified osimertinib as a candidate anti-T-ALL agent. Its efficacy and mechanism were evaluated in four T-ALL cell lines (MOLT-4, Jurkat, CCRF/CEM, and MOLT-3) with different TP53 statuses and in primary T-ALL blasts. Combination studies with selinexor, an exportin 1 (XPO1) inhibitor, were performed. Multi-omics, biochemical, and functional assays were used, and efficacy and toxicity were assessed in T-ALL xenograft models. Results Osimertinib suppressed leukemic progression in vivo by promoting proteasome-dependent degradation of c-MYC through a non-canonical, EGFR-independent pathway that cannot be fully explained by inhibition of PI3K/AKT/mTOR or NOTCH1 signaling alone. This c-MYC suppression impaired ribosome biogenesis, and combining osimertinib with selinexor further disrupted this process. The combination increased apoptosis at low concentrations (0.5-2 µM osimertinib plus 20 nM selinexor), with clear synergy at 2 µM in all four T-ALL cell lines. Mechanistically, the combination caused nuclear retention of RPS6, nuclear accumulation of RPL5/RPL11, nucleolar stress (fibrillarin dispersal), decreased MDM2 protein levels, p53 stabilization, BAX activation (6A7), cytochrome c release, c-MYC depletion, and translational suppression. In vivo, the combination improved survival and reduced leukemic burden with minimal toxicity to normal cells at low doses. Potential biomarkers include c-MYC dependency and TP53 status as candidate stratification factors, and treatment-induced c-MYC depletion and RPL5/RPL11 nuclear accumulation as candidate pharmacodynamic biomarkers. Conclusions Osimertinib plus selinexor depletes c-MYC, induces nucleolar stress, and suppresses translation, which together drive T-ALL cell apoptosis. This mechanism-driven combination shows preclinical efficacy with limited toxicity in the normal-cell and xenograft models tested. Further studies incorporating pharmacokinetic monitoring, PDX models, and prospective validation of candidate biomarkers such as c-MYC dependency, TP53 status, and RPL5/RPL11 nuclear accumulation are warranted before clinical translation.

papers.abstract: Solid tumors remain challenging for cellular immunotherapy, and CAR-T or CAR-M cells alone often have limited efficacy. Combining these approaches may improve therapeutic activity; however, our previous in vitro study observed increased IL-6, while extracellular matrix (ECM) barriers can restrict immune-cell access. We engineered IL6-CD147 CAR-M, a synthetic IL-6-responsive macrophage construct designed to couple an IL-6-binding scFv to a CD147-containing module. Following IL-6 stimulation, IL6-CD147 CAR-M showed increased MMP-2, MMP-9, MMP-11, and MMP-13 transcripts and proteins. A CD147-deletion control did not reproduce the enhanced MMP transcriptional response, and GM6001 reduced CAR-T cell migration through Matrigel toward IL6-CD147 CAR-M-conditioned medium. In defined 80:20 mixed-antigen tumor models, IL6-CD147 CAR-M plus CAR-T increased tumor killing and inflammatory/cytotoxic mediators while reducing detectable extracellular IL-6. In vivo, combined therapy reduced tumor burden, prolonged survival, increased immune-cell infiltration, altered immune composition, and was not associated with overt histopathological abnormalities in the examined major organs at the assessed time points. These findings support further evaluation of an IL-6-responsive, CD147-containing CAR-M strategy; proximal receptor signaling and the mechanism underlying reduced extracellular IL-6 remain unresolved.

papers.abstract: Human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2) is a well-established oncogenic driver in multiple solid tumors, most prominently in breast and gastric cancers. Beyond gene amplification-driven signaling through canonical PI3K/AKT and RAS/MAPK pathways, emerging evidence reveals that HER2 functions within a highly dynamic and context-dependent tumor ecosystem. Interactions between HER2-positive tumor cells and immune and stromal compartments actively shape the tumor microenvironment, contributing to immune evasion, therapeutic resistance and disease progression. A central challenge in the clinical management of HER2-altered cancers is pronounced spatial and temporal heterogeneity, which undermines both diagnostic accuracy and the durability of targeted therapies. In response, advances in multi-omics profiling, liquid biopsy technologies and artificial intelligence-assisted analytics are redefining HER2 assessment, shifting it from static tissue-based classification towards dynamic, minimally invasive monitoring. In parallel, the therapeutic landscape has evolved from single-agent HER2 blockade to rational combination strategies. In particular, antibody-drug conjugates have emerged as a transformative modality, extending the therapeutic reach of HER2 targeting beyond traditional indications and offering new opportunities to overcome heterogeneity and drug resistance. This review synthesizes current insights into the molecular and microenvironmental biology of HER2-altered solid tumors and discusses how these advances are reshaping next-generation precision oncology.

papers.abstract: Abstract Background Relapsed/refractory (R/R) lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) remains a clinical challenge with limited therapies and poor prognosis. CAR‑NK cell therapy has shown promise in solid tumors, but its efficacy is limited by both the availability of effective targets and the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment. CD73 (NT5E), highly expressed across solid tumors, catalyzes adenosine production to drive immunosuppression, representing both a specific CAR‑NK target and a key leverage point to overcome tumor immune evasion. However, its systematic evaluation as a therapeutically actionable target for CAR‑NK cell therapy in R/R LUAD remains unexplored. Methods We first characterized CD73 expression through integrative analysis of public datasets, primary and relapsed clinical LUAD specimens, and LUAD cell lines derived from primary and metastatic tumors. We then constructed CD73‑CAR‑NK cells and assessed their in vitro cytotoxicity across LUAD cell lines of varying malignancy, as well as their effects on extracellular adenosine and resistance to adenosine‑mediated immunosuppression. Finally, we assessed their antitumor efficacy in a stepwise manner across a tiered panel of in vivo models, including cell line‑derived xenograft (CDX), metastasis, patient‑derived xenograft (PDX), and clinically relevant immune‑humanized PDX models. Results CD73 expression was elevated in metastasis-derived LUAD cell lines and R/R LUAD specimens. Accordingly, CD73-CAR-NK92 cells exhibited potent cytotoxicity against CD73-high LUAD cells, accompanied by an activated effector phenotype, reduced extracellular adenosine, partial resistance to adenosine-mediated suppression, and limited activity toward normal bronchial epithelial cells. Notably, this enhanced function was consistently observed across multiple NK cell sources including peripheral blood-derived NK (PBNK), umbilical cord blood‑derived NK (UBNK), and iPSC-derived NK (iNK). In vivo, CD73‑CAR‑NK92 cells significantly suppressed tumor growth and metastasis, with enhanced tumor‑site enrichment, prolonged retention, and elevated intratumoral levels of TNF‑α and IFN‑γ. Importantly, in an immune‑humanized PDX mouse model, CD73‑CAR‑NK92 cells significantly reduced the growth of R/R patient‑derived xenografts, accompanied by immune remodeling, without marked systemic inflammation during the observation period. Conclusions These findings provide preclinical evidence that CD73-CAR-NK cells exhibit potent antitumor efficacy for R/R LUAD through their dual functions of eliminating CD73-high tumor cells and resisting adenosine-mediated immunosuppressive signaling, supporting their therapeutic potential.

papers.abstract: For more than a century after its initial description, glioblastoma (GBM) has remained one of the most therapeutically refractory human malignancies, resembling an almost impregnable fortress against modern oncology. Despite extensive molecular characterization and identification of numerous actionable targets, survival outcomes have improved only marginally. GBM is characterized by profound spatial and cellular heterogeneity, adaptive signaling rewiring, extensive phenotypic plasticity, an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment, and major pharmacological constraints imposed by the blood-brain barrier. This review examines the resulting disconnect between biological rationale and clinical outcome through three interrelated translational principles that determine whether mechanistically compelling therapies can achieve meaningful clinical benefit in GBM. First, who is treated and what is biologically active: therapeutic efficacy depends on matching patients to functional pathway dependencies beyond static molecular alterations. Second, whether the drug reaches and modulates its intended target: candidate therapies must achieve sufficient intratumoral exposure and demonstrate target modulation. Third, how the tumor adapts under therapeutic pressure: durable efficacy requires accounting for receptor tyrosine kinase switching, phenotypic plasticity, immune adaptation, and spatial escape. By linking these principles to the molecular, spatial, and pharmacological organization of GBM, this review frames the disease as a dynamic tumor ecosystem and provides a framework for interpreting recurrent clinical failure and guiding more biologically informed therapeutic development.

papers.abstract: Endometrial cancer with somatic POLE exonuclease domain mutations (EDMs) has a highly favorable prognosis; however, the clinical implications of non-hotspot EDMs in POLE remain unclear. In 793 patients with endometrial cancer enrolled at the National Cancer Center and Juntendo University Hospitals, 25 prespecified variants were screened using the Luminex assay. Whole-exome sequencing (WES) was carried out to evaluate 54 patients with hotspot and non-hotspot EDMs. In patients with endometrial cancer (n = 4864) registered in Genomics Evidence Neoplasia Information Exchange (GENIE), those harboring hotspot EDMs were matched with randomly sampled patients without EDMs, and a polymerase epsilon (POLE) score for gene panel testing was developed. In our cohort, POLE-EDMs, including hotspot (n = 91) and non-hotspot (n = 12) EDMs, were identified in 103 (12.9%) of 793 patients. The prevalence of grade 3 and advanced-stage endometrial cancer was higher in patients with non-hotspot EDMs than in those with hotspot EDMs. WES analysis of 54 patients revealed no significant differences in genomic mutations between the groups, and four non-hotspot EDMs were identified. A POLE-specific mutational signature was observed in tumors with EDM. In addition, the POLE score criteria were developed based on hotspot EDMs using the GENIE cohort, achieving a detection sensitivity of 0.94. Using the established POLE score, we identified nine non-hotspot EDMs. We identified 13 novel candidate non-hotspot EDMs using a newly established POLE score for gene panels and demonstrated an association between non-hotspot EDMs and favorable prognosis. The identification of additional non-hotspot EDMs will facilitate precise molecular classification of endometrial cancer.

papers.abstract: Cancer is the second leading cause of death worldwide and disproportionately affects older adults. As population ageing accelerates, the global cancer burden among older adults continues to increase. This study systematically evaluated the latest global cancer burden and its epidemiological characteristics among older adults. Data on the incidence and mortality of 33 malignancies, excluding non-melanoma skin cancer, among adults aged 65 + were extracted from the Global Cancer Observatory (GLOBOCAN) 2024 and Global Burden of Disease Study (GBD) 2023 databases and stratified by age, sex, region, and Human Development Index (HDI). Age-standardized incidence and mortality rates (ASIR and ASMR) were calculated. Annual percentage changes (APC) were used to characterize temporal trends. Decomposition analysis was performed to quantify the contributions of population growth, population aging, and epidemiological changes. Demographic projection methods and generalized additive model (GAM) were applied to forecast the cancer burden through 2050. In 2024, there were 9,966,392 new cancer cases and 6,001,290 cancer deaths among older adults worldwide, accounting for 51.11% and 61.84%, respectively, of all-age totals. Lung, colorectal, stomach, liver, and prostate cancers were leading causes of death. Incidence and mortality were higher in men and increased with age. The Western Pacific Region had the largest burden, whereas Europe Region had the highest ASIR. ASIR correlated positively with HDI (rs = 0.771), while mortality-to-incidence ratio (MIR) correlated negatively (rs = -0.825). From 2000 to 2023, ASIR and ASMR declined, although burden increased, primarily driven by population growth; pancreatic cancer exhibited the most rapid increase. Tobacco use remained the leading risk factor for mortality, while metabolic risks rose in importance. Under a demographic scenario assuming constant 2024 age-specific rates and changes only in population size and age structure, new cancer cases and deaths among older adults are projected to reach approximately 19.8 million and 12.5 million by 2050, roughly double the 2024 figures, with the largest increase in the Eastern Mediterranean region. Cancer burden in older adults is substantial, varying by sex, age, region, and development level. Precision prevention and control are urgently needed, particularly in low- and middle-income regions. papers.abstract: KRASG12D is a predominant driver in pancreatic cancer, yet the basis of intrinsic resistance to KRASG12D-targeted therapy remains poorly defined. Integrated genomics, transcriptomics, and proteomics profiling across 242 patient-derived organoids (PDOs) and matched tumor tissues reveals a KRASG12D-mutant subset intrinsically resistant to KRASG12D-targeted therapeutics, characterized by marked downregulation of innate immune signaling pathways. Functional validation demonstrates that suppressing interferon signaling in sensitive models induces resistance, whereas activation of interferon signaling, particularly interferon beta (IFN-β), increases sensitivity in resistant models. Combining IFN-β with KRAS inhibitors (MRTX1133, HRS-4642, and RMC-6236) exhibits synergistic antitumor effects in intrinsically resistant pancreatic cancer. Mechanistically, sustained MYC activity is associated with attenuated sensitivity to KRAS inhibition and correlates with repressed interferon signaling, suggesting a potential role in promoting intrinsic resistance. These findings identify interferon signaling as a candidate determinant of KRAS-targeted therapy response and support interferon-based combinations as a potential strategy for intrinsically resistant pancreatic cancer.

papers.abstract: Despite their considerable promise, many current medical foundation models remain modality specific and lack transparent reasoning, limiting clinical adoption. To address this gap, we introduce Explainable Vision Language Foundation Model for Medicine (EVLF-FM), a multimodal vision language foundation model that combines broad diagnostic capabilities with fine-grained explainability. The development and testing of EVLF-FM encompassed more than 1.3 million total samples from 18 global datasets across 10 imaging modalities related to six clinical specialties: dermatology, hepatology, ophthalmology, pathology, pulmonology and radiology. External validation employed 13,443 independent test samples from 17 additional datasets across 10 imaging modalities. EVLF-FM supports disease diagnosis, visual question answering and pixel-level visual grounding with reasoning capabilities. In internal validation for disease diagnostics, EVLF-FM achieved the highest average accuracy, 0.895, outperforming leading generalist and specialist models. In medical visual grounding, EVLF-FM also achieved reasonable performance across nine modalities with average accuracy at 0.5 intersection over union (Acc@0.5) of 0.842. External testing further confirmed consistent zero-shot and few-shot performance, with competitive F1 scores despite a smaller model size. A hybrid training strategy combining supervised and visual reinforcement fine-tuning enables EVLF-FM to generate clinically interpretable explanations aligned with visual evidence. Human evaluation of these reasoning outputs using the S.C.O.R.E. framework yielded a high overall mean score of 4.25/5, supporting their clinical interpretability. Current limitations include the need for additional validation across diverse healthcare settings. Prospective clinical studies are required to evaluate the safety, effectiveness and clinical utility of EVLF-FM before routine clinical deployment.

papers.abstract: The clinical adoption of deep learning in pathology is largely hindered by the "black box" nature of current models, which often obscure the biological basis of prognosis. Here, we introduce MorphX, an interpretable framework that predicts patient survival by explicitly decoding multi-scale morphological patterns from whole-slide images. Unlike conventional methods relying on latent features, MorphX fuses macro-scale tissue texture with micro-scale nuclear metrics to attribute risk to interpretable biological phenotypes. In a multi-center study spanning 1,067 patients with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD), MorphX achieves concordance indices of 0.775-0.799 in discovery cohorts. Crucially, we derive eight distinct morphology-based biomarkers-driven by texture heterogeneity in necrotic regions, lymphocyte density, and nuclear shape-that demonstrate reproducible survival associations across independent cohorts, offering a granular resolution of tumor aggressiveness that transcends traditional histological grading. By translating opaque computational predictions into validated biological insights, MorphX supports trustworthy, transparent, artificial intelligence (AI)-driven precision oncology.

papers.abstract: To evaluate the concordance between immediate post-cardiopulmonary bypass thromboelastography (TEG) findings and intraoperative transfusion practice in adult cardiac surgery. Adults undergoing cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass who had immediate post-bypass TEG performed in the operating theater. None. Manufacturer-derived TEG thresholds for fresh frozen plasma, platelets, cryoprecipitate, and procoagulant therapy were compared with observed intraoperative transfusion practice. Among 207 patients, thresholds were met in 56% for fresh frozen plasma, 20% for platelets, 17% for cryoprecipitate, and 16% for procoagulants. Intraoperative transfusion rates were higher for platelets, cryoprecipitate, and procoagulants, particularly in complex surgery, whereas fresh frozen plasma transfusion was lower than the threshold-based proportion. Among patients meeting thresholds but not receiving transfusions intraoperatively, fewer than 15% required the corresponding product within 24 hours. Postoperative chest tube output was broadly similar across TEG-transfusion patterns, with no clear association between TEG concordance and early postoperative bleeding. Substantial discordance existed between manufacturer-derived post-bypass TEG thresholds and intraoperative transfusion practice. Transfusion appeared to reflect surgical complexity more closely than measured coagulation abnormalities.

papers.abstract: The recurrent emergence of the F456L substitution in SARS-CoV-2 Omicron sublineages has been associated with immune evasion, yet its impact on vaccine-induced immune responses remains poorly understood. Using a trimeric RBD-HR subunit vaccine platform, we investigated how residue 456 influences the functional immunogenicity of the receptor-binding domain (RBD). We found that the F456L substitution markedly reduced neutralizing antibody responses against multiple SARS-CoV-2 variants, despite maintaining comparable levels of total antigen-specific IgG, indicating a selective impairment of functional immunogenicity rather than overall antigenicity. Single-cell RNA sequencing and B-cell receptor (BCR) repertoire analyses further revealed that the F456L mutation weakened germinal center responses, reduced clonal expansion, and impaired repertoire remodeling of antigen-specific B cells. Structural modeling, biolayer interferometry, and calcium flux assays demonstrated that aromatic residues at position 456 promote effective germline BCR recognition and activation. Importantly, replacing the non-aromatic leucine residue with aromatic amino acids, including tyrosine or tryptophan, restored the neutralizing antibody-eliciting capacity of the antigen. Together, these findings identify aromaticity at residue 456 as a critical determinant of RBD functional immunogenicity and demonstrate how a single amino acid substitution can reshape B-cell responses and antibody quality. This work provides important insights for rational vaccine antigen design and advances our understanding of how site-specific mutations regulate antiviral immunity.

papers.abstract: To compare remimazolam-based with propofol-based anesthesia for induction and maintenance in adult cardiac surgery. Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Cardiovascular centers. Adults undergoing cardiac surgery. Remimazolam-based versus propofol-based general anesthesia for induction and maintenance. Fourteen reports describing randomized trials, including three theses, contributed 1,773 reported participants to the primary synthesis. All were conducted in China, and no key pooled result was supported exclusively by results at low risk of bias. One terminated European registry-results trial (23 treated patients) was included as supplementary sensitivity evidence. Data on major postoperative morbidity and mortality were too sparse to pool. Across the cardiac surgical populations represented in the included trials, remimazolam was associated with fewer trial-defined intraoperative hypotension and bradycardia events and shorter mechanical ventilation duration.
